subtopics.title: Ohm's law, KCL and KVL
subtopics.theory_md:
**Ohm's law:** at constant temperature, $V = IR$.

**KCL:** the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero, $\sum I = 0$ (current in = current out). It rests on conservation of charge.

**KVL:** around any closed loop the algebraic sum of emfs equals the algebraic sum of $IR$ drops, $\sum E = \sum IR$. It rests on conservation of energy.

**Signs:** pick one direction for every branch current and one direction round each loop. A resistor met along the current is a drop, against it a rise. A battery met from $-$ to $+$ is a rise. A negative answer only means the real current is opposite.
subtopics.basics_md: Charge cannot pile up at a junction, so what flows into a node flows out. Going round a loop you return to the same potential, so the rises and drops cancel. That is all the two laws say.
key_points: KCL: $\sum I = 0$ at a node, from conservation of charge
KVL: $\sum E = \sum IR$ round a closed loop, from conservation of energy
Ohm's law: $V = IR$ at constant temperature
Sign rule: along the current a drop, against it a rise; battery $-$ to $+$ is a rise
Negative current means the actual direction is opposite to the assumed one

questions.q: In a branch-current solution you obtain $I_2 = -0.86$ A. Does this mean an error was made? What does it show?
questions.model_answer_md:
**No error.** The direction of $I_2$ was assumed at the start. A negative value means the current actually flows **opposite** to the assumed direction, with magnitude 0.86 A.

If $I_2$ is in a battery branch, the battery is **being charged** (current enters its positive terminal). The equations need not be redone.
points: Not an error: the assumed direction was only a guess
Negative sign means the real current is opposite, magnitude 0.86 A
In a battery branch it means the battery is being charged
Ohm's law: $V = IR$, current proportional to voltage at constant temperature
KCL: algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero ($\sum I_{in} = \sum I_{out}$)
KVL: algebraic sum of emfs and drops round a closed loop is zero ($\sum E = \sum IR$)
KVL: algebraic sum of voltages round any closed loop is zero
In mesh analysis one KVL equation is written per mesh
Drops in own resistors minus drops from neighbouring mesh currents in shared branches equal the emfs in the mesh
Gives the $b-n+1$ independent equations solved for the mesh currents

subtopics.title: KCL on a closed surface
subtopics.theory_md:
KCL holds not only at a node but for **any closed surface (cut-set)** drawn round part of a network: the algebraic sum of currents crossing it is zero.

**Method:**
1. Draw a closed curve that cuts only branches whose currents are known, plus the one you want.
2. Currents entering = currents leaving.
3. Currents in branches wholly inside the curve never appear.

This finds a current or voltage in one line when the circuit is large. With a known resistor current $I = (V_A - V_B)/R$, the same current must return through the rest of the cut.
subtopics.basics_md: A closed surface is just a very big node. Whatever enters it must leave it, however complicated the inside is.
key_points: KCL applies to any closed surface, not only a single node
Draw the surface so it cuts only the branches you know plus the unknown
Entering = leaving; branches wholly inside do not appear
A negative answer means the current is opposite to the arrow drawn

questions.why: $7 + 3 = 5 + I_{out}$ gives $I_{out} = 5$ A leaving.

options: only the branches inside the surface

questions.why: Only wires cutting the surface carry charge across it.

questions.q: A block of network is connected to the rest of a circuit by four wires. Three carry currents of 6 A, 2 A and 5 A into the block. Find the current in the fourth wire and its direction.
questions.model_answer_md:
KCL on the closed surface round the block: total in = total out.

$$6 + 2 + 5 = I_4 \Rightarrow I_4 = 13\ \text{A}$$

The fourth wire carries **13 A out of the block**.
points: Apply KCL to the closed surface
$I_4 = 13$ A directed out of the block
Apply KCL to a closed surface cutting only the four horizontal branches
$I_1 + I_4 + I_2 = I_3$ with arrows as drawn: $5 + I_4 + 3 = 4$
$I_4 = -4$ A, i.e. 4 A flows opposite to the marked arrow
The 7 A diagonal lies inside a section and does not enter the equation
Current in the 2 Ω from A to B: $6/2 = 3$ A
KCL on the cut round the right-hand section: the 3 A entering at B leaves at D, so 3 A flows from D to C
In the C-D branch: $I_R - 2 = 3$, so the 1 Ω carries 5 A from D to C

subtopics.title: Branch-current method (two batteries)
subtopics.theory_md:
For $b$ branches and $n$ nodes you need $b$ equations: KCL at $n-1$ nodes and KVL for $b-n+1$ independent loops (the meshes).

**Steps:**
1. Mark a current in every branch, using KCL to reduce the unknowns.
2. Write KVL for each mesh, one direction, one sign rule.
3. Solve; interpret negative values.
4. Check: the voltage of a node found by two paths must agree.

For two batteries $E_1, r_1$ and $E_2, r_2$ feeding a load $R$ in parallel, the quick form is $V = \dfrac{E_1/r_1 + E_2/r_2}{1/r_1 + 1/r_2 + 1/R}$ (Millman).
subtopics.basics_md: Unknown currents need as many equations as unknowns. KCL gives the relations between currents; KVL gives the relations between voltages. Together they are enough.
key_points: Number of independent KVL equations = $b - n + 1$; KCL equations = $n - 1$
Assume directions freely; interpret negatives at the end
Never use the outer loop together with both inner meshes: dependent set
Check by finding a node voltage along two paths

questions.why: The outer loop equation is the sum of the two mesh equations, so it adds nothing.

questions.q: Two batteries are connected in parallel across a load of 4 Ω: $E_1 = 12$ V with internal resistance 2 Ω, and $E_2 = 6$ V with internal resistance 1 Ω. Find the current in each battery and in the load.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Assume** $I_1$ (from $E_1$), $I_2$ (from $E_2$), both towards the load; load current $I_1 + I_2$.

**Loop 1:** $12 - 2I_1 = 4(I_1 + I_2) \Rightarrow 6I_1 + 4I_2 = 12$

**Loop 2:** $6 - I_2 = 4(I_1 + I_2) \Rightarrow 4I_1 + 5I_2 = 6$

Solving: $I_1 = 2.571$ A, $I_2 = -0.857$ A.

**Load:** $I_1 + I_2 = 1.714$ A.

$I_2$ is negative: 0.857 A flows **into** battery 2, which is being charged.

**Check:** $V_{load} = 4 \times 1.714 = 6.857$ V; $12 - 2(2.571) = 6.857$ V.
points: Assume branch currents and use KCL for the load current
Check with the load voltage 6.857 V

questions.q: Batteries $E_1 = 20$ V ($r_1 = 5$ Ω) and $E_2 = 10$ V ($r_2 = 10$ Ω) are in parallel across a 10 Ω load. Find the three currents and state which battery, if any, is being charged.
questions.model_answer_md:
Let the load voltage be $V$ (KCL at the top node, Millman form):

$$V = \frac{20/5 + 10/10}{1/5 + 1/10 + 1/10} = \frac{5}{0.4} = 12.5\ \text{V}$$

$$I_1 = \frac{20 - 12.5}{5} = 1.5\ \text{A},\quad I_2 = \frac{10 - 12.5}{10} = -0.25\ \text{A},\quad I_{load} = \frac{12.5}{10} = 1.25\ \text{A}$$

**Check:** $1.5 - 0.25 = 1.25$ A. Battery 2 is **charged** by 0.25 A, because the common voltage 12.5 V is above its emf 10 V.
points: Battery 2 is being charged since $V > E_2$

subtopics.title: Mesh (loop) analysis
subtopics.theory_md:
Give each window of a planar circuit a clockwise mesh current $I_1, I_2, \dots$ and write KVL round each.

A resistor shared by meshes 1 and 2 carries $I_1 - I_2$ (seen from mesh 1). By inspection:

$$\begin{bmatrix}R_{11} & -R_{12}\\ -R_{21} & R_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}I_1\\I_2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}E_1\\E_2\end{bmatrix}$$

$R_{kk}$ is the total resistance of mesh $k$, $R_{kj}$ the shared resistance. An emf is positive if the mesh current leaves its $+$ terminal. The number of equations is $b - n + 1$.

Solve by Cramer's rule, $I_k = \Delta_k/\Delta$, and show the determinants. Branch current in a shared element is the **difference** of mesh currents.
subtopics.basics_md: A mesh current is a loop of current imagined to circulate round one window. Where two windows touch, the two loops pass through the same resistor in opposite directions, so their difference is the real current.
key_points: One clockwise mesh current per window; $b - n + 1$ KVL equations
Inspection form: diagonal = own total R, off-diagonal = minus shared R
Emf positive when the mesh current leaves its + terminal
Solve by Cramer's rule or elimination; branch current = difference of mesh currents
Check by KVL in an outer path or a node voltage found two ways

questions.q: In the mesh equation for mesh 1, a resistor shared with mesh 2 contributes
questions.why: Both mesh currents are clockwise, so they oppose in the shared branch and the drop is $R(I_1 - I_2)$.

subtopics.title: Nodal analysis
subtopics.theory_md:
Choose a reference node (ground). Call the other node voltages $V_1, V_2, \dots$ and write KCL at each: sum of currents **leaving** the node = 0, each as (this voltage $-$ other voltage)$/R$. This gives $n - 1$ equations.

By inspection, $[G][V] = [I]$: the diagonal term is the total conductance at the node, the off-diagonal term is minus the conductance between the two nodes, and the right side is the source current injected into the node.

A voltage source in series with a resistor $R$ feeding a node gives the term $(V - E)/R$. Branch current $= (V_a - V_b)/R$.

Nodal suits circuits with current sources and few nodes; mesh suits many nodes and few loops.
subtopics.basics_md: The voltage at a node tells you the current in every resistor touching it. So solve for the node voltages first, then use Ohm's law.
key_points: Reference node, then $n - 1$ KCL equations
Use leaving = (this voltage $-$ other voltage)$/R$ in every term
Inspection: $G_{kk}$ total conductance, $G_{kj}$ minus shared conductance, RHS injected current
Source with series resistor: $(V - E)/R$
Finish with Ohm's law for branch currents and powers $P = (\Delta V)^2/R$

questions.q: A 24 V source with a 4 Ω resistor feeds node 1. Node 1 is joined to ground by 12 Ω and to node 2 by 6 Ω. Node 2 is joined to ground by 3 Ω and has a 2 A current source injecting into it. Find $V_1$, $V_2$ and the current in the 6 Ω.
questions.model_answer_md:
Reference = ground.

**Node 1:** $\dfrac{V_1 - 24}{4} + \dfrac{V_1}{12} + \dfrac{V_1 - V_2}{6} = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2}V_1 - \dfrac{1}{6}V_2 = 6$

**Node 2:** $\dfrac{V_2 - V_1}{6} + \dfrac{V_2}{3} = 2 \Rightarrow -\dfrac{1}{6}V_1 + \dfrac{1}{2}V_2 = 2$

Solving: $V_1 = 15$ V, $V_2 = 9$ V.

Current in 6 Ω: $(15 - 9)/6 = 1$ A from node 1 to node 2.

**Check at node 1:** in $(24 - 15)/4 = 2.25$ A; out $15/12 + 1 = 2.25$ A.
points: Current in 6 Ω is 1 A, node 1 to node 2
Reference = bottom line; node equations at node 1 and node 2
Left half: node A gives $V_A = 0.75V_J$; node J gives $V_J = 10.667$ V, so $V_A = 8$ V
Right half: the 48 V source puts its top at -48 V; node B gives $V_B = -36$ V
Nodal equations at $V_1$ and $V_2$ with the 10 A source and the 60 V source ($V_P = 60$ V)
One unknown node: the middle node, $V$
Reference D; three node equations for $V_A, V_B, V_C$ with the 1 A source into A and out of C

subtopics.title: Supermesh, supernode and source power
subtopics.theory_md:
**Current source in a mesh.** If a current source lies in a branch shared by two meshes, its voltage is unknown. Do not write KVL through it. Instead:
1. Write one KVL round the **supermesh**, the outer loop of the two meshes that omits the source branch.
2. Add the constraint $I_1 - I_2 = I_s$.

If the source is on an outer branch, that mesh current simply equals $I_s$.

**Voltage source between two non-reference nodes.** Form a **supernode**: one KCL for both nodes together, plus $V_1 - V_2 = V_s$.

**Power of a source:** $P = V \times I$ through it, with the current found from KCL at its node. A source with zero current supplies zero power.
subtopics.basics_md: An ideal current source forces its current but lets the voltage across it be whatever the circuit needs. An ideal voltage source does the reverse. So the unknown quantity in that branch is hidden, and we avoid it.
key_points: Current source shared by two meshes: supermesh KVL plus $I_1 - I_2 = I_s$
Voltage source between two nodes: supernode KCL plus $V_1 - V_2 = V_s$
Current source on an outer branch fixes that mesh current directly
Source power $P = VI$; find the current by KCL at the source node

questions.q: A 5 A current source is in the branch shared by meshes 1 and 2. The extra equation needed is
options: none, KVL through the source is enough
questions.why: The branch current is the difference of the mesh currents.

questions.q: A 6 V battery is connected between nodes 1 and 2, neither being the reference. The best method is

questions.why: A supernode removes the unknown battery current.

questions.q: Nodes 1 and 2 are joined by a 6 V source (node 1 higher). Node 1 has a 4 Ω to ground and a 9 A source injecting into it. Node 2 has a 2 Ω to ground. Find $V_1$ and $V_2$.
questions.model_answer_md:
Supernode (nodes 1 and 2) with constraint:

$$V_1 - V_2 = 6$$

KCL for the supernode: current leaving through the resistors = injected current

$$\frac{V_1}{4} + \frac{V_2}{2} = 9$$

Substitute $V_1 = V_2 + 6$: $\dfrac{V_2}{4} + 1.5 + \dfrac{V_2}{2} = 9 \Rightarrow V_2 = 10$ V, $V_1 = 16$ V.

**Check:** $16/4 + 10/2 = 4 + 5 = 9$ A.
points: Form the supernode and write the constraint $V_1 - V_2 = 6$

questions.q: Two clockwise meshes share a branch containing a 5 A current source directed downwards. Left mesh: a 24 V source and 2 Ω. Right mesh: 3 Ω and a 4 V battery opposing $I_2$. Find $I_1$ and $I_2$.
questions.model_answer_md:
The source branch is downward, which is the direction of the clockwise $I_1$, so

$$I_1 - I_2 = 5$$

**Supermesh KVL** (outer loop, omitting the source branch):

$$24 - 4 = 2I_1 + 3I_2 \Rightarrow 20 = 2I_1 + 3I_2$$

Substitute $I_1 = I_2 + 5$: $20 = 2I_2 + 10 + 3I_2 \Rightarrow I_2 = 2$ A, $I_1 = 7$ A.

points: The 3 A source across the top fixes a third mesh current, so the 5 Ω and 6 Ω carry $I_X + 3$ and $I_Y + 3$
Branch currents: 5 Ω 1.95 A, 6 Ω 0.825 A, 2 Ω 1.125 A
Power supplied by a source is $P = V \times I$ through it

Net current in the 10 V source is zero, so $P = 0$ W

subtopics.title: Thevenin's theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
**Statement:** any linear, bilateral two-terminal network can be replaced, as seen from terminals A-B, by a voltage source $V_{th}$ in series with a resistance $R_{th}$.

**Steps:**
1. Remove the load $R_L$; mark A-B.
2. $V_{th}$ = open-circuit voltage across A-B (nodal, divider or KVL).
3. $R_{th}$ = resistance seen from A-B with sources dead: **voltage sources shorted, current sources opened**, internal resistances kept.
4. Redraw $V_{th}$, $R_{th}$, $R_L$: $I_L = \dfrac{V_{th}}{R_{th} + R_L}$.

With a **dependent source**, do not switch it off: short only independent sources, apply a test source $V_t$ (or $I_t$) at A-B and take $R_{th} = V_t/I_t$. A resistor directly across an ideal voltage source, or in series with a current source, does not change $V_{th}$ or $R_{th}$.
subtopics.basics_md: Whatever the inside looks like, from two terminals a linear network behaves like one battery and one resistor. Find that battery (open-circuit voltage) and that resistor (what is left with the sources dead).
key_points: Statement: $V_{th}$ in series with $R_{th}$, linear bilateral network
Remove $R_L$; $V_{th}$ is the open-circuit voltage, found without the load
$R_{th}$: short voltage sources, open current sources, keep internal resistances
$I_L = V_{th}/(R_{th} + R_L)$; redraw the equivalent circuit
Dependent sources: test source method, $R_{th} = V_t/I_t$

questions.why: A dead current source carries zero current, which is an open circuit.

questions.q: The Thevenin voltage $V_{th}$ is measured

questions.why: It is the open-circuit voltage.

questions.q: A 30 V source with a series 6 Ω feeds terminals A-B, across which a 12 Ω resistor is permanently connected. Using Thevenin's theorem find the current in a 6 Ω load placed across A-B.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Remove the load.**

$$V_{th} = 30 \times \frac{12}{6 + 12} = 20\ \text{V}$$

**Source shorted:** $R_{th} = 6 \parallel 12 = 4\ \Omega$.

**Load current:**
$$I_L = \frac{V_{th}}{R_{th} + R_L} = \frac{20}{4 + 6} = \mathbf{2\ A}$$

subtopics.title: Norton's theorem and duality
subtopics.theory_md:
**Statement:** any linear bilateral two-terminal network can be replaced, as seen from A-B, by a current source $I_N$ in parallel with $R_N$.

- $I_N$ = short-circuit current through A-B.
- $R_N = R_{th}$ (sources dead).
- Load current by the current divider: $I_L = I_N\dfrac{R_N}{R_N + R_L}$.
- Conversion: $V_{th} = I_N R_N$.

**Steps:** remove $R_L$ and short A-B to get $I_N$; kill sources and find $R_N$; draw $I_N \parallel R_N$; reconnect $R_L$.

**Dual theorems:** Thevenin and Norton are duals. Interchange voltage and current, series and parallel, open and short, resistance and conductance, and one statement turns into the other.
subtopics.basics_md: Norton is Thevenin turned inside out. Instead of the open-circuit voltage in series with $R$, use the short-circuit current in parallel with $R$.
key_points: Norton: $I_N$ (short-circuit current) in parallel with $R_N = R_{th}$
$I_L = I_N R_N/(R_N + R_L)$ by the current divider
$V_{th} = I_N R_N$ links the two forms
Thevenin and Norton are duals: series-parallel, V-I, open-short

questions.q: An 18 V source with a 3 Ω series resistor feeds terminals A-B, across which a 6 Ω resistor is connected. Find the Norton equivalent at A-B and the current in a 4 Ω load.

$$I_L = I_N\frac{R_N}{R_N + R_L} = 6 \times \frac{2}{2 + 4} = \mathbf{2\ A}$$

**Check:** $V_{th} = I_N R_N = 12$ V, and $12/(2 + 4) = 2$ A.

subtopics.title: Superposition theorem
subtopics.theory_md:
**Statement:** in a linear bilateral network with several independent sources, the current in (or voltage across) any element is the **algebraic sum** of the values produced by each source acting alone, the others being deactivated.

**Deactivate:** voltage source becomes a short, current source becomes an open; internal resistances stay.

**Steps:** (1) mark the required current's direction; (2) for each source in turn redraw, reduce by series-parallel and use a divider; (3) add, subtracting contributions in the opposite direction.

**Limits:** valid for linear circuits and only for **voltage and current, never power**. For power, add currents first, then $I^2R$. A resistor across an ideal voltage source does not affect the rest of the circuit.
subtopics.basics_md: In a linear circuit each source does its own job independently of the others. So find what each source does alone and add the results.

Result is the algebraic sum; opposite directions subtract

questions.q: Two batteries $E_1 = 12$ V (3 Ω in series) and $E_2 = 6$ V (6 Ω in series) are connected in parallel (plus terminals together) across a 6 Ω load. Find the load current by superposition.
questions.model_answer_md:
**$E_1$ alone** ($E_2$ shorted): load and 6 Ω in parallel $= 3\ \Omega$.

$$I = \frac{12}{3 + 3} = 2\ \text{A},\quad I_L' = 2 \times \frac{6}{6 + 6} = 1\ \text{A}$$

**$E_2$ alone** ($E_1$ shorted): load and 3 Ω in parallel $= 2\ \Omega$.

$$I = \frac{6}{6 + 2} = 0.75\ \text{A},\quad I_L'' = 0.75 \times \frac{3}{3 + 6} = 0.25\ \text{A}$$

**Total:** $I_L = 1 + 0.25 = \mathbf{1.25\ A}$ (both in the same direction).

**Check:** $V = (12/3 + 6/6)/(1/3 + 1/6 + 1/6) = 7.5$ V, $7.5/6 = 1.25$ A.
points: Check by nodal: 7.5 V across 6 Ω

subtopics.title: Maximum power transfer
subtopics.theory_md:
**Statement:** a load receives maximum power from a linear DC network when $R_L = R_{th}$, the Thevenin resistance seen from the load.

**Derivation:** with the network as $V_{th}$ and $R_{th}$,
$$P = I^2R_L = \frac{V_{th}^2R_L}{(R_{th} + R_L)^2}$$
Setting $dP/dR_L = 0$ gives $(R_{th} + R_L) - 2R_L = 0$, so $R_L = R_{th}$.

$$P_{max} = \frac{V_{th}^2}{4R_{th}}$$

**Efficiency:** the source supplies $V_{th}I = V_{th}^2/2R_{th}$, so $\eta = 50\%$. Half the power is lost in $R_{th}$. Power systems run at high efficiency, not at maximum power; MPT is used in communication circuits. Find $R_{th}$ with current sources opened.
subtopics.basics_md: A small load takes little current; a large load takes little current too. In between, the product of voltage and current peaks, and that happens when the load matches the source resistance.

A 40 V source with a 10 Ω series resistor feeds terminals A-B, across which a 15 Ω resistor is connected. Find the load resistance for maximum power and that power.

**Source shorted:** $R_{th} = 10 \parallel 15 = 6\ \Omega$.

questions.q: A source has $V_{th} = 12$ V and $R_{th} = 4$ Ω. Compare the load power at $R_L = 4$ Ω and at $R_L = 12$ Ω and the efficiency in each case.

**$R_L = 12$ Ω:** $I = 12/16 = 0.75$ A, $P = 0.75^2 \times 12 = 6.75$ W (less). Efficiency $= 12/16 = 75\%$.

subtopics.title: Source transformation
subtopics.theory_md:
A voltage source $E$ in series with $R$ is equivalent, at its terminals, to a current source $I = E/R$ in parallel with the same $R$ (and back: $E = IR$).

**Use:** repeat the conversion and combine:
- Resistors in series with a voltage source add; resistors in parallel with a current source combine as parallel.
- Parallel current sources add algebraically; series voltage sources add.
- A resistor in parallel with an ideal voltage source, or in series with an ideal current source, is redundant and can be dropped.

Keep track of polarity: the arrow of the current source points towards the + end of the voltage source.
subtopics.basics_md: A battery with its internal resistance behaves the same as a current source with a resistor beside it, as far as anything outside can tell. Swap whichever form makes the next step easier.
key_points: $E$ in series with $R$ $\leftrightarrow$ $I = E/R$ in parallel with $R$
Series: add voltage sources and resistors; parallel: add current sources and conductances

subtopics.title: Delta-star and star-delta formulas
subtopics.theory_md:
Three resistors in a triangle between A, B, C form a **delta**; three joined at a common point, one to each terminal, form a **star**. They are equivalent when the resistance between every pair of terminals is the same (third terminal open).

**Delta to star:** each arm is the product of the two delta resistors touching that terminal over the sum of all three:
$$R_A = \frac{R_{AB}R_{CA}}{R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}}$$

**Star to delta:** each delta resistor is the sum of products of the star arms over the arm opposite:
$$R_{AB} = \frac{R_AR_B + R_BR_C + R_CR_A}{R_C}$$

For equal resistors, $R_Y = R_\Delta/3$.

**Derivation:** equate the resistance between A-B, B-C, C-A in both forms; subtract to solve for the star arms; multiply pairs and add to get the delta.
subtopics.basics_md: A triangle and a Y can look the same to the three outside wires. The formulas make the three pair resistances the same in both.
key_points: $\Delta \to$ Y: arm = product of the two adjacent delta resistors / sum of all three
Y $\to \Delta$: $R_{AB} = (R_AR_B + R_BR_C + R_CR_A)/R_C$
Equal resistors: $R_Y = R_\Delta/3$

questions.q: A delta has $R_{AB} = 30$ Ω, $R_{BC} = 20$ Ω, $R_{CA} = 10$ Ω. Find the equivalent star. Then convert a star with arms 2 Ω, 3 Ω, 6 Ω to a delta.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Delta to star:** $\Sigma = 60\ \Omega$.

$$R_A = \frac{30 \times 10}{60} = 5\ \Omega,\quad R_B = \frac{30 \times 20}{60} = 10\ \Omega,\quad R_C = \frac{20 \times 10}{60} = 3.33\ \Omega$$

**Star to delta** ($R_A = 2$, $R_B = 3$, $R_C = 6$): sum of products $= 6 + 18 + 12 = 36$.

$$R_{AB} = \frac{36}{6} = 6\ \Omega,\quad R_{BC} = \frac{36}{2} = 18\ \Omega,\quad R_{CA} = \frac{36}{3} = 12\ \Omega$$

questions.q: Derive the expressions for the arms of a star equivalent to a given delta.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Equivalence:** the resistance between each pair of terminals (third open) must be equal.

**Between A and B:** $R_A + R_B = \dfrac{R_{AB}(R_{BC} + R_{CA})}{R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}}$ ... (1)

**Between B and C:** $R_B + R_C = \dfrac{R_{BC}(R_{CA} + R_{AB})}{R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}}$ ... (2)

**Between C and A:** $R_C + R_A = \dfrac{R_{CA}(R_{AB} + R_{BC})}{R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}}$ ... (3)

Add (1) and (3), subtract (2), and divide by 2. With $\Sigma = R_{AB} + R_{BC} + R_{CA}$:

$$R_A = \frac{R_{AB}R_{CA}}{\Sigma}$$

and cyclically $R_B = \dfrac{R_{AB}R_{BC}}{\Sigma}$, $R_C = \dfrac{R_{BC}R_{CA}}{\Sigma}$.
points: Equate resistance between each pair of terminals, third terminal open
Add and subtract to isolate one arm

subtopics.title: Equivalent resistance of bridge networks
subtopics.theory_md:
A network that is not purely series or parallel (an unbalanced bridge) is reduced by star-delta conversion.

**Method:**
1. Label the nodes and list every element with its end nodes.
2. **Check balance** first: if $R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4$ the centre arm carries no current and can be removed.
3. Otherwise pick one delta (or star) whose conversion leaves series-parallel paths, convert it, redraw with new labels.
4. Reduce, and add the resistances in series with the terminals.
5. If another bridge appears, convert again.

Then $I = V/R_{eq}$ for the source current. Check one node voltage from both sides.
subtopics.basics_md: Pick a triangle in the middle of the tangle and swap it for a Y. The middle node disappears and ordinary series and parallel rules finish the job.

Convert one delta to star so the rest is series-parallel; redraw with node labels

subtopics.title: Series, parallel and dividers
subtopics.theory_md:
**Series:** same current, voltages add, $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots$. Voltage divider: $V_1 = V\dfrac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}$.

**Parallel:** same voltage, currents add, $\dfrac{1}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{1}{R_1} + \dfrac{1}{R_2} + \dots$. Two resistors: $R_{eq} = \dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$. Current divider: $I_1 = I\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ (the **other** resistor in the numerator).

A parallel combination is smaller than its smallest branch. Two elements are in parallel only if both ends are on the same two nodes.

**Lamps:** $R = V^2/P$. In series the lower-wattage lamp has the higher $R$, takes more power $I^2R$ and glows brighter.
subtopics.basics_md: Same current through everything means series. Same voltage across everything means parallel. Dividers just share the voltage or current in proportion to the resistances.
key_points: Series: $R_{eq} = \sum R$, same current, voltage divider
Parallel: $G_{eq} = \sum G$, same voltage, current divider with the other resistor in the numerator
Parallel equivalent is less than the smallest branch
Rated lamp resistance $R = V^2/P$; in series the lower wattage glows brighter

questions.q: A 100 W and a 60 W lamp, both rated 230 V, are connected in series across 230 V. Which glows brighter? Find the power in each.
questions.model_answer_md:
$R_{100} = \dfrac{230^2}{100} = 529\ \Omega$, $R_{60} = \dfrac{230^2}{60} = 881.7\ \Omega$.

Series current: $I = \dfrac{230}{529 + 881.7} = 0.163\ \text{A}$.

$$P_{100} = I^2R = 0.163^2 \times 529 = 14.1\ \text{W},\quad P_{60} = 0.163^2 \times 881.7 = 23.4\ \text{W}$$

The **60 W lamp glows brighter**: it has the higher resistance and the same current.
points: The 60 W lamp is brighter, higher $R$ in series

questions.q: A 100 V supply feeds 5 Ω in series with a parallel pair of 20 Ω and 30 Ω, which is in series with 3 Ω. Find the total resistance, the supply current and the voltage across the parallel pair.
questions.model_answer_md:
$20 \parallel 30 = 12\ \Omega$.

$$R_{eq} = 5 + 12 + 3 = 20\ \Omega,\quad I = \frac{100}{20} = 5\ \text{A}$$

$$V_{parallel} = 5 \times 12 = 60\ \text{V}$$

points: In parallel $R_1$ still draws 12 A, so the new resistor draws $16 - 12 = 4$ A

subtopics.title: Voltage dividers and balanced bridge
subtopics.theory_md:
Two dividers across the same supply give two midpoint voltages $V_A = V\dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ and $V_B = V\dfrac{R_4}{R_3 + R_4}$. The voltage between them is $V_{AB} = V_A - V_B$.

The bridge is **balanced** when $\dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = \dfrac{R_3}{R_4}$. Then $V_A = V_B$, $V_{AB} = 0$, and anything connected between A and B (a resistor, a galvanometer) carries **no current** and can be removed for finding $R_{eq}$:
$$R_{eq} = (R_1 + R_2) \parallel (R_3 + R_4)$$
subtopics.basics_md: If both dividers cut the voltage in the same ratio, their midpoints sit at the same voltage, so nothing flows between them.
key_points: Balanced when $R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4$: $V_{AB} = 0$
In a balanced bridge the middle arm carries no current and is removed

questions.q: Arms of a bridge across a supply are 10 Ω and 20 Ω in one branch and 15 Ω and 30 Ω in the other, with a 5 Ω between the midpoints. Find the equivalent resistance seen by the supply.
questions.model_answer_md:

subtopics.title: Reading a network: which nodes are the same
subtopics.theory_md:
Before reducing, **label the nodes**. Every point joined by a plain wire is one node.

- A resistor with **both ends on the same node** carries no current and drops out. A pair of resistors in series with both outer ends on one node does the same.
- Two wires that **cross without a dot** (a hop) do not connect: they are two separate nodes.
- Two wires that cross **with a dot** form one node.

Then the remaining elements are series and parallel between the labelled nodes. Always say how you read a crossing, since the answer changes.
subtopics.basics_md: Wires have no resistance, so everything on one wire sits at one voltage. If both ends of a resistor are at the same voltage, no current flows through it.
key_points: Label nodes; every wire-connected point is one node
A resistor (or series chain) with both ends on one node carries no current
A hop (no dot) does not connect; a dot does
